title: China and its trading partners are moving towards an economic peace. But it is a fragile one
gist: Chatham House argues China is pursuing self-interested economic stabilization with the US and EU (PHEV export limits, a ~5 mb/d cut in oil imports during the Hormuz closure), but the peace is fragile: export displacement across sectors, pressure for a stronger renminbi that would be inflationary for partners, and a $350bn EU deficit against only ~$10bn of Chinese FDI.

insights.claim: China has embraced trade 'stability' with the US and EU out of self-interest: its trading partners broadly agree China should import more and export less, and Beijing is lucky they cannot turn that shared view into coordinated policy, so it offers concessions before that luck runs out.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Treat de-escalation as tactical; a coordinated response by partners is the tail risk for China-exposed exporters.
insights.quote: Beijing is immensely lucky that its trading partners can’t turn that common view into a common policy

insights.claim: An EU-China deal in October 2026 limiting European imports of plug-in hybrid vehicles, through a WTO-compliant safeguard measure, eased trade tension and may defuse hostile trade tools France and Germany were prepared to deploy.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Lowers near-term tariff-escalation risk for European autos and Chinese EV exporters.

insights.claim: Xi and Trump agreed a period of 'constructive strategic stability' during Trump's May 2026 China visit, forming the backdrop to the EU-China deal.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: US-China bilateral tail risk is currently lowered, though the author calls it fragile.

insights.claim: China's chokepoint leverage from manufacturing dominance forces Beijing to avoid a catastrophic loss of trust among customers, because its export-led model needs those customers to stay afloat and solvent.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: China has an incentive to underwrite global demand stability, which caps how aggressive it can be.

insights.claim: Rising Western populism could take on a more explicitly anti-China hue, which adds to Beijing's motive for conciliation.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Political backlash is a latent driver of future trade measures.

themes.theme: Hormuz crisis and Chinese oil demand

insights.claim: After Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in March 2026, threatening roughly 12 million barrels per day of oil with no alternative routes, China cut crude imports sharply; by June they were down about 5 million barrels per day.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Chinese demand destruction was a major shock absorber in the oil market during the closure.

insights.claim: China's import cut reduced stress in the global oil market, supporting economic activity and limiting global inflationary pressure; the author frames this as 'strategic reasonableness' even though self-interest was at work.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Chinese import behaviour is a key swing variable for oil and inflation in supply crises.

themes.theme: Fragility and whack-a-mole in export restraint

insights.claim: The EU-China PHEV restraint creates precedent risks: other partners may demand equivalent arrangements, and EU hawks may push the same pressure onto pharmaceuticals, chemicals and machinery, where China's tolerance is likely very limited.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect trade friction to migrate to new sectors; monitor EU demands beyond autos.

insights.claim: The PHEV export surge was itself caused by the EU's tariffs on battery electric vehicles two years ago, which China sidestepped by shifting to untariffed PHEVs; with PHEVs now constrained, another manufactured export category will probably surge next.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Sectoral trade defences displace rather than reduce Chinese export volume; look for the next surge category.
insights.quote: China simply boosted its exports of PHEVs which weren’t subject to the tariffs

themes.theme: Renminbi appreciation as the likely concession

insights.claim: Beijing's manufacturing-led growth model looks unshakeable for now, so the likelier concession is letting the renminbi strengthen rather than rebalancing toward domestic spending and imports.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Positions for gradual RMB appreciation are the most plausible policy outcome of trade pressure.

insights.claim: France and Germany's unofficial trade 'non-paper' said renminbi appreciation would be a tolerable short-term substitute for deeper Chinese economic rebalancing, and US Treasury's next currency-manipulator report early next year could add pressure.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Watch the early-2027 Treasury currency report as an RMB catalyst.

insights.claim: CF40, a Chinese think-tank, estimates the renminbi's underlying equilibrium rate at about 2.5 CNY per USD on a cost-of-living-adjusted basis, versus a market rate just below 6.7.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Headroom for RMB appreciation is large on this measure, though the PPP framing is extreme.

insights.claim: A stronger renminbi would raise import prices in partner economies; the ECB has shown cheap Chinese imports keep goods inflation lower, so an RMB-induced inflation shock is unwelcome when inflation anxiety is high after the Iran war price surge since February.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Trading partners demanding a stronger RMB may be undermining their own disinflation; RMB appreciation is inflationary for the West.

themes.theme: Safe FDI as the way out

insights.claim: The US/EU-China relationship is a security dilemma, and the most hopeful exit is more 'safe' Chinese foreign direct investment abroad, which would lower China's trade surplus by shifting production to host countries.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Chinese outbound manufacturing FDI into Europe may become a policy-sanctioned path, benefiting host-country industrial assets.

insights.claim: The EU will run roughly a $350 billion trade deficit with China this year, against Chinese FDI inflows to Europe of only about $10 billion annually.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The scale gap shows how much FDI would have to grow to materially offset the imbalance.

insights.claim: The European Commission's proposed Industrial Accelerator Act is the venue where the question of Chinese FDI is now being debated, and China has a long-term incentive to park industrial assets offshore to earn investment income.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Terms of the Act on foreign ownership and local content will shape Chinese investment into EU industry.

insights.claim: Boosting Chinese FDI requires Europe to tolerate some minimal insecurity; seeking absolute security carries an economic price that will ultimately be self-defeating.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Security-screening hawkishness is a cost to European growth and industrial capacity.
insights.quote: the pursuit of absolute security will come at an economic price that is just too high
